summary: Disopyramide is a class Ia antiarrhythmic used to treat documented, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias such as sustained ventricular tachycardia. It blocks the fast inward sodium current, slowing conduction and prolonging the action potential and QT interval, and it also has potent anticholinergic and significant negative inotropic effects. Immediate-release disopyramide is usually given as about 150 mg every 6 hours (typical total 400-800 mg/day), with a controlled-release form given every 12 hours; doses must be reduced in renal or hepatic impairment and in heart failure. Key hazards are proarrhythmia (QT prolongation and torsades de pointes), worsening of heart failure due to its negative inotropy, anticholinergic effects (urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, worsening glaucoma), and hypoglycaemia. It should not be used with other QT-prolonging drugs and requires ECG and clinical monitoring.
indications: Treatment of documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, such as sustained ventricular tachycardia
Some labels include suppression and prevention of recurrence of unifocal/multifocal ventricular premature complexes and paired ventricular complexes in symptomatic patients (per product labelling)

dosage.d: Usual 150 mg every 6 hours (about 400-600 mg/day); up to 800 mg/day in some patients
dosage.t: By mouth, consistently with regard to food
dosage.n: A loading dose of 300 mg may be used (200 mg if <50 kg); reduce in renal/hepatic impairment and cardiomyopathy

dosage.d: Total daily dose given as 300 mg every 12 hours
dosage.n: Do not use controlled-release for initial rapid control; not for severe renal impairment

dosage.d: Reduce dose and extend the dosing interval according to creatinine clearance (immediate-release only)
dosage.n: Avoid controlled-release in significant renal impairment

dosage.d: Use lower doses (e.g. 100 mg every 6 hours) and monitor

admin: Initiate or adjust therapy with continuous ECG monitoring because of proarrhythmia risk, especially in higher-risk patients
Correct hypokalaemia and other electrolyte disturbances before and during treatment
Reduce dose in renal impairment, hepatic impairment, heart failure and low body weight
Swallow controlled-release capsules whole; do not use them for rapid initial control
Monitor for anticholinergic effects (urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation) and for hypoglycaemia
Avoid co-administration with other QT-prolonging drugs and check QT interval after dose changes
moa: Disopyramide is a class Ia antiarrhythmic that blocks the fast inward sodium channel in cardiac tissue, reducing the rate of phase-0 depolarisation and slowing conduction velocity. It also prolongs the cardiac action potential duration and effective refractory period (partly by potassium-channel effects), lengthening the QT interval. These actions suppress re-entrant and ectopic ventricular arrhythmias. Disopyramide additionally has marked anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity and a pronounced negative inotropic effect, which account for several of its adverse effects, including worsening of heart failure and anticholinergic toxicity.

absolute: Pre-existing second- or third-degree AV block or marked sinus node dysfunction without a pacemaker
relative: Heart failure or significant left ventricular dysfunction (negative inotropy)
Glaucoma (narrow-angle), urinary retention or prostatic enlargement (anticholinergic effects)
Renal or hepatic impairment; concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
Predisposition to hypoglycaemia (e.g. malnutrition, renal/hepatic impairment, diabetes on hypoglycaemics)
monitor: Blood pressure and signs of heart failure

preg: Disopyramide crosses the placenta; it has been associated with uterine contractions and is generally avoided in pregnancy unless clearly necessary for a life-threatening arrhythmia, using the lowest effective dose with monitoring of mother and fetus.
lact: Disopyramide and its metabolite are excreted into breast milk. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment, or the infant should be closely observed, given the potential for anticholinergic and cardiac effects.
renal: Disopyramide is substantially eliminated by the kidneys and accumulates in renal impairment, increasing the risk of toxicity and proarrhythmia. Reduce the dose and lengthen the dosing interval according to creatinine clearance; the controlled-release form should be avoided in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces clearance and increases plasma levels; reduce the dose and monitor closely for adverse effects, including QT prolongation and anticholinergic toxicity.

major: Other QT-prolonging/antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol, class Ia/III agents, some macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics) - additive QT prolongation and torsades de pointes risk; avoid
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. macrolides, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors) - raise disopyramide levels and toxicity risk
Other negative inotropes/beta-blockers/verapamil - additive cardiac depression and risk of heart failure/AV block
moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs - additive antimuscarinic effects (urinary retention, glaucoma, constipation)
Drugs causing hypokalaemia (diuretics) - increase proarrhythmia risk
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin) - lower disopyramide levels
minor: May enhance the effects of warfarin in some patients
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; keep timing consistent
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excess - may add to hypotension and hypoglycaemia
interactions.diagnostics: Causes ECG QRS and QT prolongation; can lower blood glucose on testing

common: Anticholinergic effects - dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary hesitancy/retention
serious: Proarrhythmia - QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, worsening of arrhythmia
Worsening or precipitation of heart failure (negative inotropy)
Hypoglycaemia (can be severe, especially with renal/hepatic impairment or malnutrition)
Acute urinary retention and acute angle-closure glaucoma
emergency: Torsades de pointes or other life-threatening arrhythmia
Acute decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock
Acute urinary retention or angle-closure glaucoma

monitoring: ECG (QRS and QT intervals, heart rhythm) at baseline and after dose changes
Blood pressure and clinical signs of heart failure
Blood glucose, particularly in patients at risk of hypoglycaemia
counsel: This medicine controls a serious heart-rhythm problem and needs regular heart tracing (ECG) and blood checks
Tell your doctor about dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation or difficulty passing urine - common with this drug
Report palpitations, fainting, severe dizziness, breathlessness or swollen ankles straight away
Be alert for symptoms of low blood sugar (sweating, shakiness, confusion) and treat/report them
Do not start new medicines, including some antibiotics, without checking, as they can affect your heart rhythm
Do not stop the medicine suddenly or change the dose without medical advice
pk: Antiarrhythmic effect within about 30 minutes to a few hours of an oral dose
Plasma concentrations peak about 0.5-3 hours after immediate-release dosing
Elimination half-life approximately 4-10 hours (prolonged in renal/hepatic impairment and heart failure)
Effect lasts roughly 6 hours per immediate-release dose; controlled-release allows 12-hourly dosing
Store capsules at room temperature, protected from moisture
pearls: Proarrhythmic - prolongs QT and can cause torsades; avoid other QT-prolonging drugs and correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia
Strong negative inotrope - can precipitate or worsen heart failure; avoid in significant LV dysfunction
Marked anticholinergic effects - caution in glaucoma, prostatic enlargement and urinary retention
Can cause significant hypoglycaemia, especially with renal/hepatic impairment or poor nutrition - monitor glucose
Accumulates in renal impairment - reduce dose/extend interval and avoid the controlled-release form in significant renal impairment
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, but if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose - do not take two doses together. Maintaining a steady level is important for rhythm control, so try not to miss doses.
overdose: Overdose can cause severe hypotension, widened QRS, QT prolongation with arrhythmias including torsades, bradycardia or asystole, heart failure, apnoea, loss of consciousness, anticholinergic effects and hypoglycaemia, and can be fatal. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with ECG and blood-pressure monitoring, activated charcoal if early, correction of electrolytes/glucose, inotropes/vasopressors and mechanical support for cardiac depression, magnesium/pacing for torsades, and consideration of haemoperfusion in severe cases.
